Illi vero qui carnaliter volunt vivere, cum cura carnis student et propria desideria nutrire. Ponendus est igitur utriusque modus, et cogendi sunt illi facere, quod faciendum est, pro salute. Hi vero reprimendi sunt ne faciant quod carnaliter concupiscunt. Salus quidem corporis ad serviendum Deo servanda est; cupiditas vero carnis exstinguenda est. Et quia de manifesta infirmitate locutus est, de latenti dolore subjungit, dicens:

*Denique si latens est dolor, famulo Dei dicenti quid sibi doleat, sine dubitatione credatur.*

Jure enim credendus est, quem boni mores, et conversatio sancta famulum Dei esse commendant. [0909D] Non enim ex ore loquentium cognoscitur veritas aut falsitas, sed a fructibus eorum cognoscetis eos, dicit Dominus. Non sunt fallaces, non sunt duplices; non sunt ex illis, qui in corde, et ore locuti sunt falsa. Famuli Dei quales sunt in corde, tales sunt in ore. Bona vita fidem dat verbis. Mala vita etiam ipsam veritatem facit esse ambiguam. Sine dubitatione ergo credantur qui sine dubitatione sunt boni. Alio modo: Si latens est dolor, sine dubitatione credatur. Famulus enim Dei timet Deum offendere non solum in opere, sed etiam in sermone. Tales nos exhibere debemus, ut quidquid dixerimus sine dubitatione credatur. Vita debet commendare sermonem, et opera bona testimonium perhibere veritati [0910A] sicut Salvator noster de se dicit: *Si mihi non creditis; vel operibus credite. Opera,* inquit, *quae facio, ipsa testimonium perhibent de me [n: (Joan. X)]*. Multi enim sunt quibus non creditur etiam si verum dicant, quia illi mali sunt aut in suspicione habentur ne mali sint. Sed si nostra vita sine suspicione coeperit esse bona, mox verba nostra sine dubitatione credentur esse vera. Quanto quisque minus bonus est, tanto minus ei creditur; quanto coeperit esse religiosior, tanto verbis ejus major fides praestatur. Sed quia infirmitatis necessitas aliquando appetit ea, quae sibi ipsi sunt contraria, ideo adjungit:

*Sed tamen utrum sanando illi dolori, quod delectat expediat, si non est certum, medicus consulatur.*

[0910B]Credendum est eorum verbis, nec tamen statim acquiescendum est eorum desideriis, nam et famulos Dei illicita tentant desideria; ergo si non est certum, medicus consulatur. Quaeratur ille qui de incerto faciat certum. Nec mirum si medicorum consilia quaerimus, cum apostolum Paulum consilio medicinae usum fuisse legamus. Nam per Epistolam suam Discipulo suo Timotheo praecipit dicens: *Modico vino utere propter stomachum et frequentes tuas infirmitates [n: (I Tim. V)]*. A rigore ergo abstinentiae discretus magister discipulum temperat, ne scilicet frequentibus passionibus fractus a bono praedicationis elanguescat. Bonum quippe erat ut discipulus ex infirmitate patientiae fructum redderet, sed utilius esse providebat Apostolus si usu medicinae aliquantulum [0910C] convalescens animas Deo lucrifaceret. Ex diversis autem bonis utiliora eligenda sunt. Hac autem auctoritate fulti ad haec medicinam corporalem quaerere debemus, ut inde majorem fructum Domino referamus.

*Nec eant ad balnea, sive quocunque ire necesse fuerit, minus quam duo vel tres.*

*Provideamus bona,* ait Apostolus, *non tantum coram Deo, sed etiam coram omnibus hominibus [n: (II Cor. VIII)]*. Propter nos conscientia bona sufficit nobis, propter alios fama nostra non pollui, sed pollere debet in nobis. Qui fidens conscientiae suae negligit famam suam, crudelis est, maxime in hoc loco positus, de quo dicit apostolus scribens ad discipulum: *Circa omnes teipsum bonorum operum praebe exemplum* [0910D] [n: (Tit. II)]. Rursus alibi dicit: *Speculum facti sumus mundo et angelis et hominibus. Qui nos amant quaerunt quid in nobis laudent, qui vero nos odiunt detrahunt nobis. Nos autem in utroque medio constituti adjuvante Domino nostro Jesu Christo, et vitam et famam nostram sic custodire debemus, ut non erubescamus a detractoribus laudari.* Simul ergo ire debent duo vel tres, et propter solatium et propter bonae famae testimonium. Unde Salomon ait: *Vae soli, si ceciderit non habet sublevantem; si fuerint duo, fovebuntur mutuo. [n: (Eccle. IV)]*. Bene autem ait, cum quibus praepositus jusserit ire debet, scilicet ut a praelato provideatur securitas personae et a subdito servetur virtus obedientiae.

[0911A] *Aegrotantium cura sive post aegritudinem reficiendorum, sive aliqua imbecillitate sive etiam febribus laborantium, alicui debet injungi, ut ipse de cellario petat, quod cuique opus esse prospexerit.*

Eligendus est frater timens Deum qui circa infirmos curam maximam gerat, et quod opus eis fuerit ministrare eis studeat, et eo studio et affectu eis deserviat, ac si ipsi Domino Jesu Christo deserviret. Ipse etenim dicturus est in judicio. *Infirmus fui, et visitastis me [n: (Matth. XXV)]*. Et iterum: *Quod uni ex minimis meis fecistis, mihi fecistis [n: (ibid.)]*. Debent ergo fortiores imbecillitatem portare infirmorum. Sic enim divina charitas adimpletur teste Apostolo qui ait: *Alter alterius onera portate, et sic adimplebitis legem Christi [n: (Galat. VI)]*. Lex Christi est dilectio. [0911B] Dilectionis officium est invicem onera nostra portare. Diversa vero tempora et diversae infirmitates faciunt ut onera nostra portemus invicem. Nihil autem sic probat amicum quam oneris amici portatio. Sed et ipse infirmus cui pro Dei amore servitur, debet pensare et summopere cavere ne superfluitate sua aut impatientia sibi servientem contristet. Studeat autem Deo gratias agere, ne infirmitas quae data est ei ad purgationem animae, vertatur ad augmentum culpa

*Sive autem qui vestibus sive qui codicibus praeponuntur, sine murmure serviant fratribus suis.*

Tales se exhibeant, et ea charitate fratribus suis deserviant, ne ipsi de ministerio sibi commisso peccent in murmure, nec alios per suam negligentiam [0911C] faciant murmurare. Grave peccatum est murmuratio testante Gregorio qui ait: *Regnum coelorum nullus qui murmurat accipit, nullus qui accipit murmurare poterit.* Et Salomon: *Praecordia fatui sicut rota carri [n: (Eccli. XXXIII)]*, fenum portat et murmurat. Tales ergo sunt in congregatione qui carne subditi non cessant a murmuratione. Apostolus: *Neque murmuraveritis, sicut quidam eorum murmuraverunt, et a* serpentibus *perierunt [n: (I Cor. X)]*. Quare a serpentibus, nisi quia serpens venenosus est, et omnis qui murmurat venenum diaboli habet in lingua. Jacobus.: *Lingua inquietum malum, plena veneno mortifero [n: (Jac. III)]*. *Cavendum est* ergo *nobis a murmure, ne mortifero et diabolico pereamus [0911D] veneno.*

*Codices certa hora petantur, extra horam qui petierit non accipiat.*



## CAPUT IX. DE MUNDITIA VESTIUM ET CORPORUM. (cont.)

Superius praecipit instare orationibus temporibus constitutis. Tempora ergo sunt distinguenda quibus debemus orare, et quibus debemus legere. De opere quoque alibi admonet ut nullus sibi aliquid operetur, sed omnia opera vestra in unum fiant. Haec tria commendat nobis regula quae animae nostrae valde sunt necessaria, scilicet orationem, lectionem, operationem. Nam oratione mundamur, lectione instruimur, operatione beatificamur, sicut Spiritus sanctus dicit in Psalmo: *Labores manuum tuarum quia manducabis, beatus es et bene tibi erit [n: (Psal. CXXVII)]*. Quia autem dicit ut codices singulis diebus petantur, [0912A] frequentia legendi commendatur. Frequenter debet legere servus Dei. Valde enim est utilis divina lectio. Nam per lectionem discimus quid cavere, quid agere, quo tendere debeamus. Hinc Psalmista ait: *Lucerna pedibus meis verbum tuum [n: (Psal. CXVIII)]*. Perfectionem sensus et intellectus augentur. Lectio ad orationem nos instruit et ad operationem, et nos informat ad contemplativam vitam et activam. Ideo in Psalmo: *Beatus vir,* scribitur, *qui in lege Domini* meditatur *die ac nocte [n: (Psal. I)]*. Haec sunt arma, videlicet oratio, lectio et operatio quibus diabolus expugnatur. Haec sunt instrumenta quibus aeterna beatitudo acquiritur. His armis vitia comprimuntur, his alimentis virtutes nutriuntur. Sed, etsi a lectione cessatur, debet manuum operatio subsequi, quia [0912B] otiositas inimica est animae, et antiquus hostis quem a lectione sive ab oratione vacantem invenerit, facile ad vitia rapit. Per usum namque lectionis discetis qualiter et vos vivatis et alios doceatis; per manuum operationem, et corporis macerationem, et vitiis alimenta negabitis, et vestris necessitatibus subvenietis, et habebitis unde necessitate patientibus aliquid porrigatis.

*Vestimenta vero, et calceamenta quando fuerint indigentibus necessaria dare non differant sub quorum custodia sunt, quae poscuntur.*

Hoc est quod superius dictum est, ut sine murmure serviant fratribus suis. Nequando differunt necessaria dare, faciant fratres murmurare, et sint occasio peccati. Studeant ergo servire fratribus suis [0912C] propter Deum, et necessaria congruis temporibus ministrare. Et hoc faciant sine murmure, sine tristitia, sine dilatione, cum gaudio et hilaritate, quia *hilarem datorem diligit Deus [n: (II Cor. IX)]*, ut omne quod opus est eis secundum modum congregationis, et possibilitatem loci habeant; et eis qui serviunt sit major ex inde merces a Domino. In indumentis vero et calceamentis clericorum congruus servandus est modus, ne pretiosa, vel nitida sint supra modum aut nimis abjecta et vilia; nec habentia compositionem plusquam decet, nec incompositionem ultra quam oportet. Talia ergo sint ut religionem simul commendent et honestatem. Caveant ergo fratres quibus necessaria ministrantur, ne quid expetant [0912D] importune, aut quod non deceat eorum religionem. Nam quidquid superfluum habent, mortiferum est illis. Perpendant ergo quoniam ea quae expendunt, oblationes sunt fidelium pro redemptione peccatorum. Et ideo non glorientur talibus uti, sed magis timeant, quod in Veteri Testamento de sacerdotibus dictum est, iniquitatem populi eos debere portare. Et ideo cum magno timore solliciti sint super eos quorum donis participant, quia magnum est periculum. Salubrius est autem pauperes Christi, sicut jam praedictum est, semper minus egere quam plus habere. Nam unde pauperes erimus nisi penuriam propter Deum aequanimiter portemus? Quantum ergo meminimus nos illicita commisisse, tantum oportet a licitis abstinere. Per angustam enim [0913A] portam intrare debemus, ut ad latitudinem coelestium gaudiorum pertingere valeamus. Nam quanto arctiorem vitam hic agimus, tanto majorem gloriam possidebimus in coelo.

*Lites autem nullas habeatis aut quam celerrime finiatis, ne ira crescat in odium, et trabem faciat de festuca, et animam faciat homicidam. Sic enim legitis: Qui odit fratrem suum homicida est [n: (I Joan III)]*.

Sic paulatim saepe crescunt vitia. Sane cum ab otioso verbo linguam restringere nolumus, ad noxia dilabimur; inde aliquando ad murmura et detractiones decidimus; plerumque etiam usque ad lites et contentiones; inde ad iram et odium, et juxta Salomonis vocem dum negligimus corrigere minima, prolabimur ad majora [n: (Eccli. XIX)]. Dum ergo [0913B] vitium ex vitio oritur, iniquitas prolongatur. Hinc propheta ait: *Vae qui trahitis iniquitatem in funiculis vanitatis! [n: (Isa. V.)]* Et Psalmista: *Prolongaverunt iniquitatem suam: Dominus justus concidet cervices peccatorum [n: (Psal. CXXVIII)]*. Primum est ergo omnino cavendum peccatum. Melius est enim praecavere quam emendare. Quia si per fragilitatem peccare contigerit, facile culpa corrigitur, quae cito cognoscitur. Hinc est, quod Dominus de muliere ad serpentem dicit: *Ipsa conteret caput tuum [n: (Gen. III)]*; caput serpentis conteritur, quando peccatum ibi corrigitur ubi nascitur. Debet ergo quisque esse sollicitus, ut mox ibi se studeat emendare ubi se noverit deliquisse. Quantum interest inter festucam [0913C] et trabem, tantum interest inter iram et odium. Odium enim est inveterata ira, quae quasi ex vetustate tantum accepit ut merito vetus appellaretur. Fieri enim potest ut si irascaris homini, velis etiam corrigi; si autem oderis, non potes eum velle corrigi. Per iram mentis oculus turbatur; per odium etiam exstinguitur. Unde Apostolus: *Qui odit fratrem suum in tenebris est [n: (I Joan. II)]*. Nulli irascenti videtur ira sua injusta. Unde de omni indignatione cito redeundum est ad mansuetudinis lenitatem. Nam pertinax motus facile in ejus odium transit cui non celeriter ignoscitur. Unde subditur:



## CAPUT X. DE VENIA POSTULANDA ET OFFENSA REMITTENDA.

[0913D] *Quicunque convicio, vel maledicto, vel etiam criminis objectu aliquem laeserit, meminerit satisfactione quam primum curare quod fecit, et ille qui laesus est sine disceptatione dimittere.*

Graviter offendit, qui convicio vel maledicto aliquem laedit. Apostolus ait: *Maledici regnum Dei non possidebunt [n: (I Cor. VI)]*. Et Dominus in Evangelio: *Qui dixerit fratri suo fatue: reus erit gehennae ignis [n: (Matth. V)]*. Debet ergo sicut graviter deliquit, graviter poenitere, atque ab eo quem laesit toto corde, tota humilitate veniam postulare; et ille qui laesus est sine disceptatione dimittere. Isidorus: *Qui fratrem suam tardius reconciliat, Deum sibi tardius placat.* [0914A] Frustra enim sibi Deum reconciliari atque propitiari quaerit, qui cito placare suum proximum negligit. Sed sunt quidam qui de suis meritis confidentes pigre in se delinquentibus veniam praestant; sed nihil proficit esse illaesum qui non est paratus ad veniam, dum potius haec magna sit culpa quando tardius laxantur fraterna delicta. Veritate testante didicimus quia servus, qui decem millia talenta debebat, cum poenitentiam ageret, absolutionem debiti a Domino accepit; sed quia conservo suo centum denarios sibi debenti debitum non dimisit, et hic est jussus exigi quod ei fuerat jam dimissum [n: (Matth. XVIII)]. Ex quibus verbis constat quia si hoc quod in nobis delinquitur ex corde non dimittimus, et illud rursum exigitur quod nobis jam per poenitentiam [0914B] dimissum fuisse gaudebamus.

*Si autem invicem se laeserint; invicem sibi debita relaxare debebunt propter orationes vestras, quas utique quanto crebriores habetis, tanto saniores habere debetis.*

Quotidie dicimus Deo: *Dimitte nobis debita nostra sicut et nos dimittimus debitoribus nostris [n: (Matth. VI)]*, quod si debitoribus nostris, id est eis qui in nos peccant nos dimittimus, cum dicimus Deo: *Dimitte nobis debita nostra, sicut et nos dimittimus,* ipsa nostra oratione inculpamur, et Deum adversum nos ad iracundiam incitamus, et ipsi super nos inducimus maledictionem potius quam benedictionem. Sicque fit ut oratio quae debebat nobis esse salubris, sit noxia, et peccata nostra quae debuimus minuere, orando augeamus. [0914C] De quotidianis autem levibus brevibusque peccatis sine quibus haec vita non ducitur quotidiana oratio fidelium satisfaciet. Eorum est enim dicere: *Pater noster qui es in coelis [n: (ibid.)]*, qui jam tali Patri regenerati sunt ex aqua et Spiritu sancto. Delet omnino haec oratio minima quotidianaque peccata. Delet et illa a quibus vita fidelium etiam scelerate gesta, sed poenitendo in melius mutata discedit. Sed quemadmodum veraciter dicitur: *Dimitte nobis debita nostra* (quoniam non desunt quae dimittantur), ita veraciter dicatur, *sicut et nos dimittimus debitoribus nostris.* Idem fiat quod dicitur; quia et ipsa eleemosyna est veniam petenti homini ignoscere. Multa quidem genera sunt eleemosynarum, quae cum facimus adjuvamur ut dimittantur nobis peccata [0914D] nostra. Sed ea nihil est majus qua ex corde dimittimus quod in nos quisque peccavit. Minus magnum est erga eum benevolum esse sive etiam beneficum qui tibi nihil mali fecerit, illud multo grandius et magnificentissimae bonitatis est ut tuum quoque inimicum diligas, et ei qui tibi malum vult semper bonum velis, facias quoque quod possis audire dicentem Jesum: *Diligite inimicos vestros, benefacite his qui oderunt vos, et orate pro eis qui vos persequuntur [n: (Matth. V)]*. Sed quoniam perfectorum sunt ista filiorum Dei quo se debet omnis fidelis extendere, et humanum animum ad hunc affectum orando Deum et secum agendo luctandoque perducere; tamen quia hoc magnum bonum tantae multitudinis [0915A] non est quantum nos creamus exaudiri cum in oratione dicitur: *Dimitte nobis debita nostra sicut et nos dimittimus debitoribus nostris,* procul dubio sponsionis hujus verba implentur si homo qui nondum ita proficit ut etiam diligat inimicum, tamen quando rogatur ab homine qui peccavit in eum ut ei dimittat, dimittit, ex corde, quia etiam sibi roganti utique vult dimitti cum orat et dicit: *Dimitte nobis sicut et nos dimittimus debitoribus nostris,* id est sic dimitte nobis rogantibus debita nostra, sicut nos dimittimus rogantibus debitoribus nostris. Jam vero qui eum in quem peccavit hominem rogat, si peccato suo movetur ut roget, non est adeo deputandus inimicus, ut eum sic diligere sit difficile, ut difficile erat cum inimicitias exercebat. Quisquis autem roganti [0915B] et peccata sua poenitenti ex corde non dimittit, nullo modo existimet a Domino peccata sua dimitti, quoniam mentiri Veritas non potest, quae ait: *Si dimiseritis hominibus peccata eorum, dimittet vobis et Pater vester coelestis delicta vestra [n: (Matth. VI)]*.

*Melior est autem qui, quamvis ira saepe tentetur, tamen impetrare festinat ut sibi dimittat cui se fecisse agnoscit injuriam, quam qui tardius irascitur et ad veniam petendam tardius inclinatur.*

Nonnullos ira citius ascendit et facilius deserit, nonnullos vero tarde commovet, sed diutius tenet. Alius autem (quod nequius est) et citius iracundiae flammas accipit et tardius deponit. Nonnulli vero has et tardius suscipiunt et citius amittunt. In quibus [0915C] nimirum liquido lector agnoscit quia ad tranquillitatis bonum ultimus plus quam primus accedit, et in malo secundum tertius superat. Quanta sit ergo iracundiae culpa pensemus, per quam dum mansuetudo amittitur, similitudo supernae imaginis vitiatur. Per iram justitiam relinquitur, sicut scriptum est: *Ira viri justitiam non operatur [n: (Jac. I)]*. Per iram gratia vitae socialis amittitur, sicut scriptum: *Noli esse* assiduus *cum homine iracundo, ne forte discas semitas ejus et sumas scandalum animae [n: (Prov. XXII)]*. Nam qui se humana ratione non temperat, necesse est ut bestialiter solus vivat. Aliquando autem ira manus non exerit, sed in maledictionis jacula linguam vertit. Nonnunquam vero [0915D] dum accensus animus a consueta locutione restringitur, per accessum temporis penitus a proximi dilectione separatur, et acriores stimuli ad mentem veniunt, causaeque quae gravius exasperent oriuntur, atque in irati oculo festuca in trabem vertitur, dum ira in odium permutatur. Veremur a proximis despici, dedignamur injurias verbi tolerare, si contingat jurgium fortasse cum proximo, erubescimus priores satisfacere. Cor quidem carnale dum hujus vitae gloriam quaerit, humilitatem respuit, et plerumque ipse homo qui irascitur discordanti sibi reconciliari appetit, sed ire ad satisfaciendum prior erubescit. Pensemus ergo facta capitis nostri, ut videamus quo jaceant nostrae pravitatis errores. Ecce inter nos et Deum peccando discordiam fecimus, [0916A] et tamen ad nos Deus suos negatos prior misit, ut nosipsi qui peccavimus ad pacem Dei revocemur. Erubescat ergo humana superbia, et confundatur quisque si non satisfaciat proximo, quoniam post culpam nostram ut ei reconciliari debeamus, et ipse qui offensus est legatis intervenientibus obsecrat Deus.

*Qui autem non vult petere veniam aut non ex animo petit, sine causa est in monasterio, etiamsi inde non projiciatur.*

Cum Dominus tantum curae reconciliationis nostrae habeat, ut patiatur munera sua derelinqui ante altare et imperfecta manere atque interrumpi ministeria sua, donec eas et resolvas iracundiam et disjungas inimicitias cum fratre tuo, nec nos ipsum [0916B] erubescimus, sed dies multos patimur manere inimicitias, et trahimus sicut funem longam discordiam. Non iracundos tantum et malitiae memores punit Deus, sed et eos qui irascentes offendunt aut placare negligunt atque contemnunt. Quoniam quidem hi qui passi sunt et videntur pati injurias, necessario dolent et irascuntur; qui vero fecerunt, nec doloris aliquid nec iracundiae gerunt. Ob hoc ergo hunc qui ab iracundia liber est adducit ad illum qui in dolore est, et liber non est, ostendens quia criminis hujus noxa penes hunc magis est qui causam peccati dedit. Sed nec sic quidem emendamur. Persistimus enim pro rebus nullis contristare fratres nostros, et quasi nil mali fecerimus de satisfactione negligimus, et oblivioni tradimus culpam atque in [0916C] longum tempus protrahi patimur, ignorantes quod tanto largior nobis erit poena, quanto largior discordia. Ubi enim amicitia permanet, nihil facile recipitur, nihil facile creditur quod dissidium possit operari. Si vero semel inimicitiae occupaverint, omnia quae fiunt, quae dicuntur, quae audiuntur, ita accipiuntur et ita intelliguntur ut ad majores et longiores proficiant inimicitias. Si quid autem mali, hoc solum creditur et confirmatur. Jubet ergo Dominus relinqui donum ante altare et prius reconciliari fratri, ut ex hoc discamus quia si nec illo in tempore quo ad ministerium Dei jubemur accedere, reconciliationem dissimulari ac differri patitur Deus, quanto magis curanda sit haec in aliis temporibus. [0916D] Si forte accidat irasci, mandatur ut sub die aut iracundiam nostram vel inimicitias nostras finiamus. In hoc constringimur praecepto quo ait: *Sol non occidat super iracundiam vestram [n: (Ephes. IV)]*. Nos contra nec hoc contenti sumus ut iracundiam ultra solis terminum producamus, sed et insidias invicem instruimus sive rebus sive verbis supplantare cupientes proximos, mordentes invicem et comedentes, quod utique aperta insania est. Quid enim aliud faciunt insani et daemone repleti, nisi membra sua morsibus dilaniant? Frustra est ergo in monasterio qui discordat cum fratre suo, quia nec Deum placat sacrificiis nec proficere valet operibus bonis.

*Proinde vobis a verbis durioribus parcite.*

Salomon: *Responsio mollis frangit iram sermo [0917A] durus excitat furorem [n: (Prov. XV)]*. Itemque: *Dulce verbum inimicos mitigat, et amicos multiplicat [n: (Eccli. VI)]*. Et Paulus: *Vos qui spirituales estis, instruite hujusmodi in spiritu lenitatis [n: (Galat. VI)]*. Caveant ergo viri sancti a verbis duris.

*Quae si emissa fuerint ex ore vestro, non pigeat ex ore proferre medicamenta, unde facta sint vulnera.*

Primum quidem summopere caveamus ne duris verbis aliquem conturbemus, quod si aliquando peccamus ex fragilitate, oportet continuo ad satisfactionem venire, et contra sermonem durum proferre dulcem atque placabilem, ut vulnus commotionis sanet medicina humilis confessionis. Sed sicut praediximus: *Melius est ante cavere vitium quam postea emendare commissum.* Ideo servus Dei debet [0917B] semper ponere custodiam ori suo, ut non delinquat in lingua sua, et tunc maxime quando adversus eum consistit peccator, videlicet aliquis calumniosus ac injuriosus, sicut scriptum est: *Sunt multi superbi et invidi qui non cessant irritare famulos Dei [n: (Eccli. V)]*. Ergo si est tibi intellectus, responde proximo tuo: *Sin autem, sit manus tua super os tuum ne capiaris verbo indisciplinato et confundaris [n: (Eccli. V)]*.



## CAPUT X. DE VENIA POSTULANDA ET OFFENSA REMITTENDA. (cont.)

*Quando autem necessitas disciplinae moribus coercendis dicere vos dura verba compellit, si etiam ipsi modum vos excessisse sentitis, non a vobis exigitur ut a vobis subditis veniam postuletis, ne apud eos quos oportet esse subjectos, dum nimium servatur humilitas, regendi frangatur auctoritas.*

Plerumque hoc magnis doctoribus contingit ut [0917C] dum coacta correctione fervent, modum correctionis exaggerent, et lingua aliquid, quae non debet, dicat, quia mentem dilectio quantum debet non inflammat. Unde bene per Moysem Dominus praecepit, dicens: *Si quis abierit cum amico suo simpliciter in silvam ad ligna caedenda, et in succisione lignorum securis fugerit manum, ferrumque lapsum de manubrio amicum ejus percusserit et occiderit, hic ad unam supradictarum urbium confugiet, et vivet, ne forte proximus ejus cujus est effusus sanguis doloris stimulo prosequatur et apprehendat eum et percutiat animam ejus [n: (Deut. IX)]*. Ad silvam quippe cum amico imus quoties cum quolibet proximo ad intuenda delicta nostra convertimur, et simpliciter ligna [0917D] succidimus, cum delinquentium vitia pia intentione resecamus. Sed securis manum fugit, cum sese increpatio plusquam necesse est in asperitatem protrahit, ferrumque de manubrio prosilit, cum de correctione sermo durior excedit, et amicum percutiens occidit, quia auditorem suum prolata contumelia a spiritu dilectionis interficit. Correcti namque mens ad odium proruit si hunc immoderata increpatio plusquam debuit addicit. Sed is qui incaute lignum percutit et proximum exstinguit, ad tres necesse est urbes fugiat ut in una earum defensus vivat. Quia si ad poenitentiae lamenta conversus in unitate sacramenti sub spe, fide et charitate absconditur, reus perpetrati homicidii non tenetur, eumque exstincti proximus cum invenerit non occidit. Quia [0918A] et justus ille judex qui se pro nobis per naturae suae consortium conjunxit, ab eo procul dubio vindictam de culpae reatu non expetit, quem sub ejus venia fides, spes et charitas abscondit. Ideo subjungitur:

*Sed tamen petenda est venia ab omnium domino, qui novit eos quos plus justo forte corripitis, quanta benevolentia diligatis.*

Aliquando exceditur modus zelo malitiae, aliquando zelo justitiae, plerumque ex studio per deliberatam locutionem, plerumque per excessum locutionis. Dominus vero non tam attendit sermonem quam intentionem. Citius ergo culpa dimittitur quae nequaquam malitiae studio perpetratur.

*Non autem carnalis sed spiritualis inter vos debet [0918B] esse dilectio.*

Sunt nonnulli qui diligunt proximos, sed per affectum cognationis et carnis, quibus tamen in hac dilectione sacra eloquia non contradicunt. Sed aliud est quod sponte impenditur naturae, aliud quod ex praeceptis Dominicis ex charitate debetur obedientiae. Hi nimirum et proximum diligunt, et tamen illa sublimia dilectionis praemia non assequuntur, quia amorem suum non spiritualiter, sed carnaliter impendunt. Omnipotentis Dei esse discipulos sola custodia charitatis probat. Unde ipse ait: *In hoc cognoscent omnes quia discipuli mei estis, si dilectionem habueritis ad invicem [n: (Joan. XIII)]*. Quae dilectio si cor nostrum veraciter replet, duobus modis ostendi solet, si amicos in Deo et inimicos diligimus propter [0918C] Deum. Saepe in dilectionis imagine erga inimicum animus fallitur, seque illum diligere falso arbitratur. Sed tunc inimici dilectio veraciter custoditur, cum nec de profectu addicimur nec de ruina laetamur. A duobus quidem praeceptis incipit charitas, sed sese ad innumera extendit. Hujus namque initium dilectio est Dei et proximi, sed Dei dilectio per tria distinguitur, quia ex toto corde et ex tota anima et ex tota fortitudine conditor diligi jubetur.

Qua in re notandum est quod divinus sermo cum Deum diligere praecipit, non solum narrat, sed etiam informat ex quanto cum subjungit: Ex tota fortitudine, ut videlicet qui perfecte Deo placere desiderat, sibi de se nihil relinquat. Proximi autem dilectio [0918D] ad duo praecepta derivatur. Unde dicitur: *Quod tibi non vis fieri vide ne tu alteri facias [n: (Tob. IV)]*. Et per semetipsam Veritas dicit: *Quae vultis ut faciant vobis homines et vos facite illis [n: (Matth. VII)]*. Quibus duobus scilicet utriusque Testamenti mandatis per unum malitia compescitur, per aliud benignitas praerogatur, ut quod non vult malum pati quisque, non faciens cessat a nocendi opere; et rursum bonum quod sibi fieri appetit, impendens ad utilitatem proximi exerceat ex benignitate. Sed haec nimirum duo dum sollicita intentione cogitantur, cor ad innumera virtutum ministeria tenditur, ne vel ad inferenda quae non debet in desideriis inquieta mens ferveat, vel erga exhibenda quae debet otio resoluta [0919A] torpescat. Nam cum cavet alteri facere quod nequaquam vult ab altero tolerare, sollicita se intentione circumspicit, ne superbia elevet et usque ad despectum proximi animum dejiciens exaltet. Ne ambitio cogitationum laniet, cumque hanc ad appetenda aliena dilatat, angustet; nec luxuria polluat et subjectum desideriis per illicita corrumpat. Ne ira exasperet et usque ad proferendam contumeliam inflammet. Ne invidia mordeat, et alienis felicitatibus aemula sua se face consumat. Ne immoderate linguam loquacitas pertrahat, eamque ad lasciviam obtrectationis extendat. Ne odium malitia excitet, et os usque ad jaculum maledictionis irritet. Rursumque cum cogitat ut ea alteri faciat quae sibi ab altero fieri exspectat, nimirum ut malis bona, ut [0919B] bonis meliora respondeat, ut erga procaces mansuetudinem longanimitatis exhibeat, ut malitiae peste languentibus gratiam benignitatis impendat, ut discordes pace muniat, ut concordes ad concupiscentiam verae pacis accendat, ut indigentibus necessaria tribuat, ut errantibus viam rectitudinis ostendat, ut afflictos verbo et compassione mulceat, ut accensos in hujusmodi desideriis increpatione restringat, ut minas potentium ratiocinatione mitiget, ut oppressorum angustias quanta praevalet ope levet, et foris obsistentibus opponat patientiam, ut intus superbientibus exhibeat cum patientia disciplinam, ut erga subditos sic mansuetudo zelum temperet, quatenus a justitiae studio non declinet, si ad ultionem zelus ferveat, ne tamen pietatis limitem [0919C] fervendo transcendat, ut ingratos quosque ministeriis in amorem attrahat, ut proximorum mala cum corrigere non valet taceat, ut quaecunque corrigi possunt consensum esse silentium pertimescat, ut sic ea quae tacet toleret, nec tamen in animo virus doloris occultet, ut sic malevolis munus benignitatis exhibeat, ne tamen per gratiam a jure rectitudinis excidat, ut cuncta proximis quae praevalet impendat, sed impendendo non tumeat, ut sic in bonis quae exhibet tumoris praecipitium caveat, ne tamen et boni exercitio torpescat, ut sic quae possidet tribuat, ut quanta sit largitas remunerantis attendat, nec cum terrena largitur suam plus quam necesse est inopiam cogitet, et in oblatione muneris claritatis lumen tristitia obscuret. Bene ergo lex Dei multiplex [0919D] dicitur, quia nimirum una eademque charitas si mentem plene coeperit, ad innumera opera multiformiter accendit. Multiplex ergo ista lex est Dei quae singulis hic rerum articulis non permutata congruit, et causis se variantibus non variata conjungit. Cujus nimirum legis multiplicitatem bene Paulus ostendit, dicens: *Charitas patiens est, benigna est,* etc. [n: (I Cor. XIII)].



## CAPUT XI. DE OBEDIENTIA.

*Praeposito tanquam Patri obediatur, multo magis presbytero qui omnium vestrum curam gerit.*

Obedientia sola virtus est quae caeteras virtutes inserit menti, insertasque custodit. Samuel: *Melior [0920A] est obedientia quam victima [n: (I Reg. XV)]*; quia per victimas aliena caro, per obedientiam vero voluntas propria religatur. Salomon: *Vir obediens* loquitur victorias [n: (Prov. XXI)], quia dum voci alienae humiliter subdimur, nos in corde superamus. Nobis quippe obedientia usque ad mortem servanda praecipitur. Per obedientiam malum nunquam fieri, aliquando autem etiam debet per obedientiam bonum quod agitur, intermitti. Sed quia nonnunquam nec jubentur adversa, sciendum summopere est quod obedientia aliquando si de suo habeat aliquid, nulla est, aliquando autem si de suo non habeat aliquid, minima est. Nam cum hujus mundi successus praecipitur, cum locus superior imperatur, is qui ad percipienda haec ex proprio desiderio anhelat, obedientiae [0920B] sibi virtutem evacuat. Rursum cum mundi despectus praecipitur, cum probra et contumeliae adipisci jubentur, nisi haec ex semetipso animus appetat, obedientiae sibi meritum minuit, quia ad ea quae in hac vita despecta sunt, invitus nolensque descendit. Debet ergo et obedientia in adversis aliquid ex suo habere, et rursum in prosperis ex suo aliquid omnino non habere, quatenus et in adversis tanto sit gloriosior, quanto divino ordini etiam ex desiderio jungitur, et in prosperis tanto sit vilior, quanto a praesenti ipsa, quam divinitus percipit, gloria funditus ex mente separatur. Innocuis autem mentibus ornamentum semper obedientiae jungitur, Domino attestante qui ait: *Oves meae vocem meam audiunt, et ego agnosco eas, et sequuntur me [n: (Joan. X)]*. [0920C] Profecto Redemptori obedit qui innocens est; et innocens esse non potest qui obedire contemnit.

*Ut ergo cuncta ista serventur, et si quid minus servatum fuerit non negligenter praetereatur, sed ut emendandum corrigendumque curetur, ad praepositum praecipue pertinebit, ut ad presbyterum, cujus est apud vos major auctoritas, referat quod modum vel vires ejus excedit.*

Ad hoc quidem data sunt ista regularia praecepta ut cuncta serventur, et si quid minus servatum fuerit, oportet ut cito emendetur. Non enim possumus aliquid praeterire negligenter sine periculo animae nostrae. Etenim vovimus specialiter tenere, et secundum ea vivere juravimus. Et Psalmista ait: *Tu mandasti mandata tua custodiri nimis [n: (Psal. CXVIII)]*. Et [0920D] apostolus Jacobus: *Si quis autem totam legem servaverit, offendat autem in uno, factus est omnium reus [n: (Jac. II)]*. Pertinebit ergo ad praepositum et ad eum qui custos est ordinis, ut ad presbyterum cui major est auctoritas, id est ad abbatem referat quidquid per se secundum canonicam regulam non potest definire. Quod si in congregatione ubi est ordo canonicus non est abbas sed episcopus, ipse episcopus presbyteri nomine designatur. Ad hoc enim praelati constituti sunt in Ecclesia ut bene ordinata custodiant, errata corrigant, vitam et mores subditorum verbo et exemplo componant, Apostoli formam sectantes qui ait: *Argue, obsecra, increpa [n: (I Tim. IV)]*. Immiscentes temporibus tempora, terroribus blandimenta, [0921A] indisciplinatos et inquietos debent durius arguere, obedientes, mites et patientes ut in melius proficiant obsecrare. Negligentes, contemnentes, et superbos aut increpent aut puniant. Neque dissimulent peccata delinquentium, sed mox ut coeperint oriri, radicitus ut praevalent, amputent, memores periculi Heli sacerdotis de filiis suis. Honestiores atque intelligibiliores prima et secunda admonitione corripiant; improbos et duros corde, superbos et inobedientes verbere et castigatione coerceant, reducentes illud in memoriam: Stultus verbo non corrigitur, percute filium tuum virga, et liberabis animam ejus a morte [n: (Prov. XXIII)].

*Ipse vero qui vobis praeest non se existimet potestate dominante, sed charitate serviente felicem.*

[0921B]Nam qui ita praesunt ut gaudeant de potestate dominii, non sunt veri pastores, sed mercenarii; hi magis praeesse appetunt quam prodesse, non quaerunt animarum fructum, sed temporale lucrum; non coelestem gloriam, sed terrenum honorem. De talibus ait Dominus in Evangelio: *Amen dico vobis, receperunt mercedem suam [n: (Matth. VI)]*. Qui vero ita praesunt ut gaudeant de servitute charitatis, ipsi tenent exemplum veri pastoris, qui non venit ministrari sed ministrare et animam suam dare redemptionem pro multis. Illi vere praelati sunt et secundum Deum curam regiminis agunt, qui ad hoc tantum laborant, ut plures ad Deum secum trahant, quos delectat onus non honor, charitas non potestas, servitus impensa aliis, non suscepta ab aliis. [0921C] Juxta quod Apostolus ait: *Cum essem liber in omnibus, omnium me servum feci, ut omnes lucrifacerem [n: (I Cor. IX)]*. Qui tamen propter auctoritatem regiminis honorandus est a subditis. Unde et subditur:

*Honore coram vobis praelatus sit vobis.*

Ideo scilicet, honorari debet, quia Christi vocem in monasterio tenet. Unde et ipse Dominus pastoribus ait: *Qui vos audit me audit, et qui vos spernit me spernit [n: (Luc. X)]*. Debent ergo servi Dei suum honorare magistrum, cujus pro amore Dei supra se susceperunt magisterium. Qui tamen quanto plus honoratur exterius, tanto oportet ut amplius timeat, atque semetipsum despiciens eos a quibus honor impenditur sibi in cogitatione praeponat. Unde subjectum est:

[0921D] *Timore coram Deo sit substratus pedibus vestris.*

Hinc scriptum est: *Quanto major es, humilia te in omnibus [n: (Eccli. III)]*. Et iterum: Fili, te ducem constituerunt, *noli extolli,* sed *esto in* eis *quasi unus ex* illis [n: (Eccli. XXXII)]. Et Dominus in Evangelio: *Omnis qui se exaltat humiliabitur, et qui se humiliat exaltabitur [n: (Luc. XVIII)]*. Tanto quippe est major quisque apud Deum, quanto humilior fuerit apud semetipsum. Sed qualis debeat esse in moribus audiamus.

*Circa omnes seipsum bonorum operum praebeat exemplum.*

Sicut enim praecellit honore et dignitate et ordine, ita eos praecedere debet sanctitate, ut ejus exemplo discant subditi qualiter vivere debeant.

[0922A] *Corripiat inquietos, consoletur pusillanimes, suscipiat infirmos, patiens sit ad omnes.*

Qui locum tenet regiminis, mala inferre non debet sed tolerare, ut ex sua mansuetudine iracundos valeat mitigare. Quia medicus animarum contra passiones vitiorum debet opponere medicamenta virtutum, ita scilicet ut prius mores omnium diligenter inquirat, ut quid cuique inferre debeat agnoscat.

*Disciplinam libens habeat, metuendus imponat. Et quamvis utrumque sit necessarium, tamen plus a vobis amari appetat quam timeri, semper cogitans Deo se pro vobis redditurum esse rationem.*

Oportet ut doctor ecclesiasticus sapiens sit et disciplinatus, quia tunc aliis recte disciplinam imponit, cum ipse disciplinate vivit, cum ex seipso trahit [0922B] magisterium quod exercet in alio. Verba sunt Apostoli dicentis ad Hebraeos: *In disciplina perseverate, tanquam filiis offert se vobis Deus. Et quis filius quem non corripit pater? [n: (Hebr. XII.)]* Sunt autem haec duo necessaria ut rector suis exhibeat subditis, timorem scilicet et amorem. Timorem iis qui superbi hac rebelles et durae mentis sunt. Amorem vero eis qui libenter, humiliter et devote serviunt Domino Deo.

*Et quamvis utrumque sit necessarium, tamen plus a vobis amari appetat quam timeri.*

Quia praelatus, quanto plus diligitur, tanto plus auditur. Et magis placet Deo illa servitus, quae ex voluntate et amore fit, quam illa quae fit ex timore. Propterea dulcis magister discipulis suis ait: *Jam [0922C] non dicam vos servos, sed amicos [n: (Joan. XV)]*. Non enim vult Dominus ut eum tanquam Dominum timeamus, sed vult ut eum diligamus tanquam patrem filii, et ut praecepta ejus faciamus, non timore poenae sed amore justitiae. Hoc semper autem cogitare debet qui judex est animarum, quia super se judicem habet Deum, ut regiminis curam tanto sollicitus agat, quanto strictius se redditurum rationem pro sibi commissis apud districtum judicem pensat. Valde enim sollicitus debet esse quisque in bono opere, ut in cunctis quae agit semper cogitet de extremo fine. Unde scriptum est: *In omnibus operibus tuis memorare novissima tua, et in aeternum non peccabis [n: (Eccli. VII)]*.

*Unde vos magis obediendo non solum vestri, sed etiam [0922D] ipsius miseremini, qui inter vos quanto in loco superiori, tanto in majori periculo versatur.*

In periculo magno versatur, quisquis in regiminis loco sublimatur. Nam quanto superior gradus, tanto periculosior casus, et cui plus committitur, plus ab eo exigitur. Grande periculum est sibi et aliis vivere, temporalia simul et spiritualia providere. Sic debet sui curam agere, ut alios non negligat, sic de aliis cogitare, ut semetipsum obliviscendo non derelinquat; sic temporalia procurare, ut non refrigescat a spiritualibus. Sic inardescere ad spiritualia, ut sit sollicitus de temporalibus. Inde ergo magis subditi praelato obedire debent, unde magis eum pro ipsis vident laborare. Quod cum faciunt non sui, sed etiam [0923A] ipsius magis obediendo miserentur. Sui videlicet; quia animas suas salvant. Scriptum est enim: *Miserere animae tuae placens Deo [n: (Eccli. XXX)]*. Ipsius quoque qui praeest miserentur; quia onus ejus alleviant obediendo. Cum enim scriptum sit: *Filius sapiens laetificat patrem [n: (Prov. X)]*; tanto plus gaudent et liberius laborant Patres spirituales pro filiis, quanto magis eos vident spiritualibus obtemperare disciplinis.

*Donet Dominus ut observetis haec omnia tanquam spiritualis pulchritudinis amatores, et bono Christi odore de bona conversatione fragrantes, non sicut servi sub lege, sed sicut filii sub gratia constituti.*

Apte subditur post lectionem oratio. Sic enim est legere et praedicare, quomodo agrum seminare; [0923B] sic orare, quomodo semen operire. Sicut qui seminant in agro si hoc operire dissimulaverint, veniunt volucres, et totum quod seminatum esse videbatur diripiunt; ita quidem isti qui in agro sui cordis semina verbi. Dei psallendo, legendo, praedicando, asperserint, nisi postea orando in corde recluserint et quodammodo sepelierint, veniunt volucres, id est cogitationes hujus saeculi volatiles inanes et vacuae, et rapiunt quod in corde fuerit seminatum. Ideo post lectionem et praedicationem semper orandum est, ut virtus verbi Dei maneat in corde, et fructus spiritualis crescat in operatione. Bene autem ait:

*Tanquam spiritualis pulchritudinis amatores.*

Non enim possunt implere haec omnia regularia praecepta nisi per amorem justitiae, quae est spiritualis [0923C] pulchritudo animae. Nemo enim invitus bene agit, etiam si bonum est quod agit. Quod vero subdit:

*Et bono Christi odore de bona conversatione fragrantes.*



## CAPUT XI. DE OBEDIENTIA. (cont.)

Pertinet ad bonam vitam et bonam famam. Unde Apostolus: *Christi bonus odor sumus Deo in omni loco [n: (II Cor. II)]*. Servi sunt sub lege, qui ex timore Domino serviunt; liberi sub gratia, qui ex amore implent divina mandata. *Gratia Dei diffusa est in cordibus nostris per Spiritum sanctum qui datus est nobis [n: (Rom. V)]*: implet legem: *Justo non est lex posita [n: (I Tim. I)]*; *ubi enim spiritus Domini, ibi libertas [n: (II Cor. III)]*. Sic autem viam mandatorum Dei curremus libere, si dilatatum cor nostrum in charitate [0923D] Dei habeamus.

## CAPUT XII. DE JUGI MEDITATIONE REGULAE.

*Ut autem vos in hoc libello tanquam in speculo possitis [0924A] inspicere, ne per oblivionem aliquid negligatis, semel in septimana vobis legatur.*

Ideo legi praecipitur, quatenus memoriter frequenter teneatur. Beatus enim Jacobus dixit: *Qui perspexerit in lege perfectae libertatis, et manserit in ea, non auditor obliviosus factus sed factor operis; hic beatus in facto suo erit [n: (Jac. I)]*. Et bene hunc libellum dicit speculum; quia in eo tanquam in speculo inspicere possumus quales sumus, sive pulchri, sive foedi, sive justi, sive injusti; utrum quisquam nostrum regulariter vivat; utrum proficiat, an deficiat; utrum Deo placeat an displiceat. Scriptura quippe nobis sacra nostram interiorem repraesentat imaginem; ostendit quid formosum, quid deforme sit in anima, et qualiter pulchritudo justitiae debeat observari, qualiter [0924B] debeat virtutum decor componi; quomodo vitiorum macula debeat abstergi. Pravorum usus est mala semper tegere, et quae egerint nunquam retractare. Quidquid faciunt caeca mente pertranseunt. At contra sancti viri in Scripturis sacris quotidie non cessant inspicere vitam suam, moresque suos vigilanter pensare. Et si quid deforme vel incompositum aut inordinatum invenerint, mox quod secundum scriptum vident, reformare et componere se student: quatenus sancti et immaculati coram Deo tam in corpore inveniantur quam in anima. Ideo Psalmista ait: *Tunc non confundar cum perspexero in omnibus mandatis tuis [n: (Psal. CXVIII)]*. Et Apostolus admonet, dicens: *Renovamini spiritu mentis vestrae [n: (Ephes IV)]*. Et iterum: *Noster homo interior renovatur de die in [0924C] diem [n: (II Cor. IV)]*. Unde aperte subjungitur:

*Et ubi vos inveneritis ea quae scripta sunt facientes, agite gratias Deo bonorum omnium largitori.*

Gratiarum actiones Patri *luminum* semper a nobis debentur, a quo *omne datum optimum et omne donum perfectum [n: (Jac. I)]*. Scriptura teste descendit. Nemo est enim donis Dei beatus qui donanti existit ingratus. Et Apostolus: *Quid habes quod non accepisti? [n: (I Cor. IV.)]* Merito ergo Domino Deo nostro gratias agere admonemur, ut agnoscat homo si quis bene vivit gratia Dei se habere, et ut proficiatur in dilectione justitiae non aliunde consecuturum. Quae cogitatio pium facit. Ipsa est enim sapientia quae pietas vocatur, qua colitur Pater luminum. Colitur autem sacrificio laudis gratiarumque actionibus, ut [0924D] cultor ejus non in seipso sed in Domino glorietur.

*Ubi autem sibi quicunque vestrum videt aliquid deesse, doleat de praeterito, caveat de futuro, orans ut ei debitum dimittatur, et in tentationem non inducatur.*
english:
## CHAPTER ONE. ON THE LOVE OF GOD AND OF NEIGHBOR. ON UNITY OF HEARTS, AND COMMUNITY OF GOODS.

[0881A]

These precepts which are written below are called a rule for this reason, namely because in them the norm of living rightly is set forth for us. And it is called a rule because it rules rightly, or because it teaches rightly. And what we call a rule, the Greeks call a canon. Whence also by a Greek name those have been called canons, that is, regulars, who, established in monasteries, live canonically and apostolically according to the regular precepts of the holy Fathers; and to them it is said.

*These are the things which we command you, who are established in the monastery, to observe.*

To this end the divine precepts are read to us, that [0881B] once read they may be understood and fulfilled. That sentence is to be feared in which it is said: *The servant who knows the will of his lord and does it not shall be beaten with many stripes [n: (Luc. XII)]*. Hence Paul says: *For not the hearers of the law, but the doers shall be justified [n: (Rom. II)]*. Let us therefore hear the sacred precepts of our loving Lord, and let us be mindful of his commandments so as to do them. For as blessed James says: *If any man hath looked into the law of perfect liberty, and hath continued therein, not becoming a forgetful hearer but a doer of the work, this man shall be blessed in his deed [n: (Jacob. I)]*. And the Lord in the Gospel: *Blessed are they who hear the word of God and keep it [n: (Luc. XI)]*. Therefore let us humbly attend to the things which are commanded us who are established in the monastery.

*First, the reason for which you are gathered into one is that [0881C] you may dwell of one mind in the house, and that there be for you one soul and one heart in God.*

First an admonition is made to us concerning unity and concord; [0882A] and concerning such concord as is made in God. For concord for the doing of sin is evil; but concord for the doing of good, and for the pursuit of justice, and for the service of God, is good. This is the reason for which we are gathered into one, namely that in the divine service we all may have [sic: *hain domo*] one spirit and one soul, and that there be for us one soul and one heart in God. For it behooves that, if we are gathered into one bodily, we should dwell together spiritually as well. For it profits nothing if one house contains us and a differing will divides us. For God attends more to unity of mind than of place. Behold, in one house we are many men, of different characters, different hearts, different souls. All these one intention and one love toward God ought to join into one. We ought [0882B] therefore to be of one mind and one will in this, that we may serve God and love God with our whole heart and with our whole soul, and our neighbor as ourselves. And so the virtue of concord is necessary for us, which can be had thus: if a brother, when he comes to the monastery, begins to strip himself of his own will, and to imitate him who says: *I came not to do my own will [n: (Joan. VI)]*. And again: *Father, not as I will, but as thou [n: (Matth. XXVI)]*. For this is what most of all brings in concord, if each man strives to do not his own but another's [sic: *veluntatem*] in what is good. And this is the judgment of great humility. Thence obedience is born, charity grows, and peace and justice, and the virtues of the Church; whereas if I wish to do my own will, and that man his, divisions arise, quarrels spring up, angers too [0882C] and brawls, which are the works of the flesh. And as the Apostle says: *They who do such things shall not obtain the kingdom of God [n: (Galat. V)]*. There are some in the congregation [0883A] [sic: *beamus*]. And therefore he commands that we dwell of one mind, obstinate in their own opinion, wise in their own eyes; for what they have conceived in their mind, this they defend as though from reason; and they contend not that they be joined to others, but that others be joined to themselves. And if they see that they are not complied with, they are at once stirred up and thrown into confusion. Such men are wont to be rebels against the commands of their elders; and in them the passion of disobedience and of impatience reigns most of all. These are not fit for concord. *For,* according to the Apostle's word, *they became vain in their thoughts, and their foolish heart was darkened; for professing themselves to be wise, they became fools [n: (Rom. I)]*. Pride indeed is a great darkness of the heart, and it is a very foolish wisdom to wish to prefer oneself to others. Against which the same Apostle says: *If any man among [0883B] you seem to be wise, let him become a fool, that he may be wise [n: (I Cor. III)]*. For the fool is wise, and according to God it is great wisdom to judge oneself inferior to all. Whence it is written: *The greater thou art, the more humble thyself in all things [n: (Eccli. III)]*. Hence the Lord at once recalls his disciples, among whom there was a contention which of them should seem to be the greater, to the concord of humility, saying: *He that is the greater among you, he shall be your servant. And the Son of man himself came not to be ministered unto, but to minister, and to give his life a redemption for many [n: (Matth. XX)]*. Therefore let us dwell of one mind in the house. *For it is good and pleasant to God for brethren to dwell in unity [n: (Psal. CXXXII)]*. Nor do our fastings, our prayers, please him so much as concord does. Therefore he says in the Gospel: *Go [0883C] first to be reconciled to thy brother, and then coming thou shalt offer thy gift [n: (Matth. V)]*. From which words it is plain that he who has not concord is not able to offer sacrifice to almighty God. We ought therefore to weigh how great is the virtue of concord in God's sight, without which not even those sacrifices are pleasing by which sins are blotted out. And it is to be known that when we come to conversion we take up a contest against the devil. But there is nothing that he fears so much as the unity of charity. For if we distribute all that we have for God's sake, the devil does not fear this, because he himself possesses nothing. If we fast, he does not dread this, because he takes no food. If we keep vigil, he is not terrified by it, because he uses no sleep. But if we are joined [0883D] in charity, at that he is vehemently afraid, because we hold on earth what he scorned to keep in heaven. Hence it is that holy Church is described as though she were terrible as an army of camps set in array, because just as enemies are afraid when they see the battle line of a camp well ordered and joined together for war, so without doubt the devil takes fright when he beholds spiritual men, girded with the arms of the virtues, living in the unity of concord; and being conquered he grieves vehemently, since he is not able to divide them through discord and to penetrate them. Hence it is written of the Lord: *His place was made in peace [n: (Psal. LXXV)]*. There he broke the powers, the bow, the shield, the sword, and war. From which words it is plain that concord breaks all the arms of the devil.

[0884A] *And let there be for you one soul and one heart in God.*

These are the firstfruits of the spirit, which from the beginning of our conversion we ought to offer to almighty God, as Wisdom herself commanded, saying: *Son, give me thy heart [n: (Prov. XXIII)]*. For first we are drawn to God by heart and by will. Therefore if we are separated in body from the world, let us be joined to God in heart and soul, that we may be able to say truly: *But for me it is good to cleave to God. For he who cleaves to God is one spirit with him [n: (Psal. LXXII; I Cor. VI)]*. Let us therefore cleave to him, that we may be strong through him, that we may be one in him, and blessed with him may say to him: *My soul hath cleaved after thee [n: (Psal. LXII)]*. Charity separates us from the world, and it is she who joins us to God. So there will be for us one soul, and one heart in God, if with our whole [0884B] heart and with our whole soul we love God. For *God* indeed *is charity, and he who abides in charity abides in God, and God in him [n: (I Joan. IV)]*. And because charity seeks not the things that are her own, it is rightly subjoined:

*And say not that anything is your own, but let all things be common to you.*

For we ought not to have anything as our own, nor to call anything "mine," but "ours," so that it is said our cope, our tunic, our house, and likewise in the rest. For we ought to have all things in common, and to call all things by a common name.

But in this it is to be weighed how great a difference there is between carnal brothers and spiritual ones. For those divide what [0884C] is common to them; these put into common what had been divided. There each man seeks what is his own; these seek not the things that are their own, but the things that are Jesus Christ's. This kinship therefore is worth more than that; because that one fails, this one grows. That has division, this unity. That passes away with the present world, this abides with the world to come. For to this end we now live together in this house, that afterward we may abide in the heavenly kingdom. *We are the sons of God,* says the Apostle, *but it hath not yet appeared what we shall be. But we shall know, when he shall have appeared, we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is [n: (I Joan. III)]*; and Paul: *We have not here a lasting city, but we seek one to come [n: (Hebr. XIII)]*. Therefore we ought not to have things of our own, but let all things be [0884D] common to us. Men make portions for themselves in this world: one silver and gold; others houses and households: one a great name, power and glory; this man this, another another, different men in a different way. But the portion of the godly is God himself. And if we wish to have such a portion, such an inheritance as the Lord is, we must show ourselves such that we may be worthy to possess him and to be possessed by him. Therefore if we wish to possess God as our inheritance, we ought to have nothing outside God. For he is exceedingly greedy for whom God does not suffice. For if we seek anything whatever — gold, for example, silver, possessions — the Lord disdains to be made a portion along with such portions. The words are Jerome's: *I,* he says, *do not receive an inheritance among the other tribes; but as a priest and a levite live [0885A] by tithes; and serving the altar, I am sustained by the offering of the altar: having food and clothing, with these I shall be content.--For blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven [n: (Matth. V)]*. And because, as long as we live here, we stand in need of bodily necessity, it is rightly subjoined.

*And let food and clothing be distributed to each of you by your prior.*



## CHAPTER ONE. ON THE LOVE OF GOD AND OF NEIGHBOR. ON UNITY OF HEARTS, AND COMMUNITY OF GOODS. (cont.)

For thus the Lord willed his Churches to be ordered, that some should have leisure for spiritual things, and others should minister temporal things to them. And therefore he willed some to be priors, others subjects. It is the office of priors to minister bodily things to their subjects. It is the ministry of subjects to devote themselves to spiritual studies: to be free for reading, for prayer, for contemplation, to serve the heavenly Lord in psalms, hymns and spiritual [0885B] songs. There is therefore all the more need that they live the more carefully with regard to themselves, inasmuch as the care of others' affairs does not entangle them. It has been established by the Lord that they who serve the altar should live by the altar: *The laborer is worthy,* as he himself says, *of his hire [n: (Luc. X)]*. And therefore, if we live on the provision of Christ, it is also just that we should labor in the service of Christ: and then we worthily receive our hire, if we have first been good laborers. For the apostle Paul says: *He who will not work, let him not eat [n: (II Thess. V)]*. Because if we do not labor and yet eat, we are made guilty of the greater crime the more we receive God's benefits unworthily. It behooves us therefore to serve him by whom we are fed, if without peril to the soul we wish to take what is distributed; and we ought to be the more careful [0885C] in good work, the more we receive these things without great labor. For what wonder is it if those who are occupied with temporal affairs live less studiously and religiously, if they frequently offend in their thoughts and words and actions? For the use of the world draws a man to sin even sometimes against his will. But those to whom both the care of the world and the occasion of sinning are lacking, the less religiously they live, the more they offend the judge on high: nor do they offend, even in the smallest negligences, without grave peril to the soul. Let us therefore weigh to what end food and covering are bestowed on us: that our whole desire may be *first to seek the kingdom of God and his justice, for the sake of which all these things are added unto us [n: (Matth. VI)]*. But in what manner it is to be distributed is shown when it is [0885D] added below.

*Let it not be distributed equally to all, because you are not all equally strong, but rather to each one according as each shall have need.*

And this he strengthens by apostolic authority, saying:

*For so you read in the Acts of the Apostles, that they had all things common, and it was distributed to each one as each had need [n: (Act. IV)]*.

This is not to be understood as though what was needful to each were distributed so abundantly that they should have no want. For although it is written that *among them there was none in want [n: (Act. IV)]*, we also read it written of the apostles themselves that they served God *in hunger and thirst, in cold and nakedness [n: (II Cor. XI)]*. [0886A] From which words it is to be gathered that many are in want in body, not in mind. But they who deny themselves for Christ's sake overcome nature itself by strength of mind. For the love of God, which is strong as death, extinguishes not only unlawful desires but even those bodily and natural affections themselves. In the primitive Church indeed there was so great an abundance of spiritual grace, that they were not only content with little but reckoned this very thing, that they had nothing, as the highest delights. Whence the Apostle says: *Having nothing and possessing all things [n: (II Cor. VI)]*. Hence also a certain holy man says: *Our poverty sufficed us, that* it should be reckoned riches [n: (Tob. V)]. Again the Apostle says: *Great,* he says, *is the gain of godliness with sufficiency; having,* he says, *food and clothing, with these let us be [0886B] content [n: (I Tim. VI)]*. In matters of this kind, therefore, we ought not to attend to the will of the flesh, but to the strength of nature. For the carnal will craves more than necessity does. Wherefore, in that which is said, that to each be given what he has need of, this measure is to be kept: that the flesh be so nourished that it may serve, and again so restrained that it may not grow proud; that the necessity of nature be so preserved that the superfluity of concupiscence be cut away.

*But let those who had anything in the world, when they have entered the monastery, willingly wish it to be common.*

This the brethren of the primitive Church did. For it seemed worthy to them that they who had a common grace should have a common substance also; and that they [0886C] whose spirit was one should have one expense also. And the word *willingly* is well added, because *God loves a cheerful giver [n: (II Cor. IX)]*. Willingly ought we to give earthly things, that we may be able to purchase heavenly ones. For the kingdom of heaven is worth as much as you have. Nothing is cheaper when it is bought, nothing dearer when it is possessed. There are two things which must be left for God's sake, namely the means of possessing and the will of having. Hence it is that the Lord says in the Gospel: *He who renounces not all that he possesses cannot be my disciple [n: (Luc. XIV)]*. And again: *He who will come after me, let him deny himself [n: (Luc. IX)]*. The former pertains to substance, the latter to the will. For it is not enough to leave outward substance, unless we cut away inward concupiscence. [0886D] Whence it is also added:

*But let those who had nothing not seek in the monastery those things which they could not have outside either.*

Even those who had nothing outside have within them something which they can leave for God's sake, namely the will of having. Whence it is written: *Thou shalt not covet [n: (Exod. XX)]*. For God attends more to the affection than to the assessment. Hence it is said by the Wise Man: *Son, give me thy heart [n: (Prov. XXIII)]*. Which cannot be done unless carnal appetite be first cut back. First, then, we are bidden to forsake what we have; then not to seek earthly things, that afterward we may be able the more freely to pant after heavenly ones. And lest it should seem that to the poor of the world who are converted the necessities ought not to be ministered, [0887A] because they are commanded to seek nothing in the monastery, it is subjoined:

*But nevertheless let what is needful be given to their weakness, even if their poverty, when they were outside, could not find even the necessities themselves.*

For whether they be rich or poor, whether noble or ignoble, whoever come to the service of Christ, it is just that they live on the provision of Christ. *For the laborer is worthy of his hire [n: (I Tim. V)]*.

*Yet let them not on that account think themselves happy, because they have found food and covering such as they could not find outside.*

For many come to conversion not so much for the soul's salvation as for the body's necessity; [0887B] who worship not God but their own belly, of whom the Apostle says. *Whose God is their belly [n: (Philipp. III)]*. To such the Lord says in the Gospel: *Amen I say to you, you seek me not because you have seen signs, but because you have eaten of my loaves [n: (Joan. VI)]*. The whole intention and happiness of such men is that they may be well fed, well clothed, and that it may go well with them in temporal things. And because they crave earthly things, they are deprived of heavenly ones. *For they have received,* as the Lord says, *their reward [n: (Matth. VI)]*. Wherefore it is above all to be guarded against, that we cleave not to temporal goods. Therefore the Psalmist admonishes us, saying: *If riches abound, set not your heart upon them [n: (Psal. LXI)]*. Earthly things indeed ought to be in our use, but heavenly things in our desire. For there is a certain wonderful and great multitude [0887C] of the sweetness of God which he has in himself, of which it is said: *That eye hath not seen, nor ear heard, neither hath it entered into the heart of man, what God hath prepared for them that love him [n: (I Cor. II)]*. Whence it is written: *I shall be satisfied when thy glory shall appear [n: (Psal. XVI)]*. That satisfying, therefore, ought to be our happiness.



## CHAPTER II. ON HUMILITY.

*Nor let them lift up the neck, because they are made companions of those whom they did not dare to approach outside; but let them have the heart on high and not seek vain earthly things, lest monasteries begin to be useful to the rich and not to the poor, if the rich are humbled there and the poor are puffed up.*

To lift up the neck is a sign of pride. If heaven was not useful to the proud [0887D] angels, it is certain that the monastery will not be useful to proud men. And though the place be holy, though the habit be holy, though the works appear holy, the whole will be held useless by reason of the vice of pride. For pride has a fall. Therefore holy David prays to the Lord that *the foot of pride come not to him, because there they fell who work iniquity: they were cast out, and could not stand [n: (Psal. XXXV)]*. On the contrary, monasteries are useful to the humble. For they are the teachable of God, as it is written: *He will teach the meek his ways [n: (Psal. XXIV)]*. And likewise: *Who* sends forth *springs in the valleys [n: (Psal. CIII)]*; that is, he bestows his grace on the humble. These indeed do not lose the good things they do, because they do not forsake humility, the guardian of the virtues. And because, according to the evangelical precept, [0888A] they recline in the lowest place, and according to the prophet choose to be abject in the house of the Lord, they therefore deserve to be heard by him, as it is written: *Everyone who exalts himself shall be humbled; and he who humbles himself shall be exalted [n: (Luc. XVIII)]*. And again: *God resists the proud; but to the humble he gives grace [n: (I Petr. V)]*.

*Again also let those who seemed to be something in the world not hold their brethren in disdain, who came to that holy society out of poverty. But rather let them study to glory not in the dignity of rich parents, but in the fellowship of poor brethren.*

Above all must the brethren guard, who have come to a holy society and a common life, that the one hold not the other in disdain, however much richer he be than him, [0888B] or nobler, or wiser. Since, as the Apostle says: *God hath chosen the weak things of the world and the ignoble and the contemptible, that no flesh should glory in his sight [n: (I Cor. I)]*, namely neither the powerful in his power; nor the wise in his wisdom, nor the rich in his riches. *For there is no respect of persons with God [n: (Colos. III)]*. For the same Lord is rich unto all who call upon him. And we are well bidden to glory not in the dignity of rich parents but in the fellowship of poor brethren, since he who is rich in his glory was made poor for us. He deigned to be made a companion not of the rich but of the poor; that we too may be poor for his sake, since to the poor the kingdom of heaven has been promised. To glory in riches indeed pertains to the vanity [0888C] of the world; but to glory in poverty pertains to blessedness.

*Nor let them be exalted if they have contributed something of their means to the common life; nor let them be prouder of their riches because they share them with the monastery, than if they will enjoy them in the [sic: *saecuto*].*

From the preceding sentence and from those which follow, two kinds of pride are marked out for us. One carnal, the other spiritual. For to disdain the poor and to glory in nobility pertains to that pride which is wont frequently to occur among worldly men. To exalt oneself over works of mercy is spiritual pride, which is wont to corrupt even spiritual men. And spiritual pride is more to be feared than carnal, [0888D] because to exalt oneself over a good work or over a virtue is to fall from a height. And the higher the ascent, the more perilous the fall. The Lord says in the Gospel: *When thou dost alms, let not thy left hand know what thy right hand doeth, that thy alms may be in secret; and he who seeth in secret will repay thee [n: (Matth. VI)]*. By the right hand is signified right working; by the left, the world's favor and self-exaltation; from these words we are admonished to be zealous to hide the right things we do from self-exaltation, otherwise we shall not have our reward with our Father. Then he shows how great is the vice of pride, when he subjoins.

*For any other iniquity whatsoever is exercised in evil works, that they may be done; but pride lies in wait even for good works, that they may perish.*

[0889A]From this it appears that pride is greater than the other vices. For through vices and virtues it drives out the human mind; pride is hateful to God and to men, of which it is written: *Pride is the beginning of every sin [n: (Eccli. X)]*. It is first in sinning; it remains last in the struggle. For when the servant of God has overcome the other vices, and has already climbed to the heights of the virtues, he still has a fight against pride, and unless he has vanquished her, he has labored in vain in the rest. When therefore we do good things outwardly, let us guard the heart within from self-exaltation; because no work with pride is pleasing to God. Whence Scripture admonishes us, saying: *With all watchfulness* keep *thy heart, because death and life proceed from it [n: (Prov. IV)]*.

*And what does it profit to scatter and give to the poor and [0889B] to become poor, when the wretched soul is made prouder by despising riches than it had been by possessing them?*

It profits us nothing to leave our own things, unless we leave ourselves also. For the Lord does not say: *Blessed are the poor* in goods, but *in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven [n: (Matth. V)]*. From the contempt of things each man ought to be more humble, not prouder; and it would be better that he keep them in the world than so to leave them that he grow proud of it in the monastery. Just as, therefore, that soul is blessed which divides its own goods among the poor for the Lord's sake, that it may be humbled, so is that one wretched which is exalted thereby. Unhappy indeed is he who by the way of the virtues makes for the vices, and from that whence he ought to have had a reward, from that he incurs a torment. For every proud man is as much in [0889C] the depth as he raises himself on high, and slips the more deeply the more loftily he is lifted up. Certain vices having been cut away, he returns to that oneness of mind which he commended first, saying.

*All of you therefore live of one mind and in concord, and honor God in one another, whose temples you have been made.*

We live of one mind if we have one mind in God, just as the primitive Church, whose heart was one and soul one. That he says *of one mind* pertains to the will. But that he adds *in concord* pertains to good manners. This is the right order of living: first that the will be one, then that the life be concordant. The brother who wishes to live in concord ought first to lay aside depraved manners, lest he be perverse, disordered, [0889D] undisciplined, lest by his anxiety he oppress the rest; then he ought so to balance his acts and his whole life that he may be able to be in concord, according to God, with those among whom he lives. There are therefore not a few who, after they leave the world, wish to follow their own wills. And again there are very many who in their acts desire to appear as worldly men. Therefore it is said: All of you therefore live of one mind and in concord. And we honor God in one another if we love one another for his sake, if we carefully keep his precepts and are made his holy temple by the indwelling of his Spirit in us. It is ours to honor God; it is God's to dwell in us and to enlighten us by grace

[0890A] *Nor let them be exalted if they have contributed something of their means to the common life,* etc., as far as *they were enjoying them.*

It is better to keep one's goods in the world than so to distribute them in the monastery as to wish to be exalted thereby. For if they are exalted, they are cast down. For whoever swells up in that which he does well, by that very path by which he advances he falls. For a good action with self-exaltation does not lift up but weighs down. Blessed therefore is that soul which can say with the Prophet: *Lord, my heart is not exalted, neither are my eyes lifted up, neither have I walked in great matters, nor in wonderful things above me [n: (Psal. CXXX)]*. Plainly happy is he who has no hidden pride in the heart, nor open pride in the body, nor in the countenance, nor in the habit, nor in speech, nor in work, nor in the rest of his motions. And if he does not [0890B] walk in great matters, that is, if he does not reckon himself among the great, on the ground that he was noble or powerful, or that he contributed his riches to the common life, or that he is useful in some office. And if he does not walk in wonderful things above himself, so as not to wish to appear as one admirable and praiseworthy on account of the religion and sanctity conferred upon him from above by God. Yet rarely is anyone found who has not some stirring from these things. But that the servant of God may be able to overcome all these kinds of pride, he ought always to think humbly of himself and not to exalt his soul, but to hold it down in humility, according to what is written: *The greater* thou art, *the more humble thyself in all things [n: (Eccli. III)]*. For the words that follow are greatly to be feared: *For any other [0890C] iniquity whatsoever,* etc. For avarice is not exercised except in evil works. Luxury is not exercised except in evil works, and likewise the other vices. Pride alone lies in wait even for good works, that they may perish. Therefore the Pharisee lost his good deeds, because he boastfully declared that he had done them. Augustine: There are some who glory the more vainly over the contempt of vain glory. Likewise there are very many who are the more vainly exalted over the contempt of riches, concerning whom it is subjoined:

*And what does it profit to scatter and give to the poor and to become poor, when the wretched soul is made prouder by despising riches than it had been by possessing them?*

As if he were openly saying. What does poverty profit with pride? Better is a humble rich man than a proud poor man. Better is a humble sinner than a just man [0890D] puffed up. In all things, therefore, the servant of God ought to be provident and circumspect: first, that he do no evil; then, that he neglect no good; afterward, that he swell not up in us over what he does; because those things which we do are truly good if we always guard them in humility And then we are truly the poor of Christ, if we are humble for the love of Christ. And: *Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven [n: (Matth. V)]*. Whence it is openly subjoined:

*All of you therefore live of one mind and in concord, and honor God in one another, whose temples you have been made.*

Poverty indeed and humility beget charity. And charity nourishes unity; and unity and [0891A] concord make us the temple of God. And then we truly honor God, when we live of one mind and in concord. For then we show that we are the disciples of Christ, if we hold the unity of the charity of Christ. Hence it is that the Lord says: *In this all men shall know that you are my disciples, if you have love one for another [n: (Joan. XIII)]*.



## CHAPTER III. ON PRAYER AND FASTING.

*Be instant in prayers at the appointed hours and times.*

To pray before the time is foresight. To pray at the appointed time is obedience. To let the time of praying pass by is negligence. Prayer ought to be the more frequent, the more useful it is. We ought to pray instantly and ardently. For great are the good things which God promises us. [0891B] For *eye hath not seen, nor ear heard, neither hath it entered into the heart of man, what God hath prepared for them that love him [n: (I Cor. II)]*. He does not wish his good things to grow cheap through ease in seeking and finding them. Precious and [sic: *desirabilis*] merchandise seeks out an eager trader. Therefore the Lord exhorts us in the Gospel, saying: *Ask, and it shall be given you; seek, and you shall find; knock, and it shall be opened to you [n: (Matth. VII)]*. For the kingdom of God is not promised to the idle, the lukewarm and the negligent, but, as Scripture says: *The kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and the violent bear it away [n: (Matth. XI)]*. God loves instancy and importunity in prayer. If the good things are great, the desires ought not to be small. With the greatness of the rewards the greatness of the desires ought to agree. But if at the first tears the Lord does not hear, not even so [0891C] is one to desist from seeking and knocking; but rather one must persevere with such instancy, and the Saviour must be besought with so obstinate a cry, until he fulfils the desire of him who prays. But if any of us feels that his conscience or his thought or his action is defiled with the filth of vices, he ought to implore the mercy of the Redeemer with continual laments, and to ask the intercessions and help of the saints; and if after the example of the woman of Canaan we persist in praying and remain fixed, the grace of our Redeemer will be at hand, to correct all our errors in us, to sanctify unclean things, to calm troubled ones. For he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, to cleanse us from all iniquity, if we cry to him with the assiduous voice of the mountain. And that the brethren may be able to pray secretly and [0891D] quietly, it is therefore subjoined:

*Let no one do anything in the oratory except that for which it was made, whence also it received its name, so that if perhaps some wish to pray outside the appointed hours (if they have leisure for it), those who think something is to be done there may not be a hindrance to them.*

Therefore our Lord cast the sellers and buyers out of the temple, saying: *My house shall be called the house of prayer [n: (Matth. XXI)]*; to teach that in the Lord's house nothing else is to be done but to pray. For to this end every church is established, that in it prayer be made. For it is the house of God and the gate of heaven. There sinners are reconciled, and the just are sanctified; there the divine mysteries are accomplished and the heavenly sacraments are handled. [0892A] Whence Solomon says: Lord, if thy people shall be converted and shall pray toward thy sanctuary, thou wilt hear them and wilt forgive their sins [n: (III Reg. VIII)]. And therefore it is above all to be guarded against, that nothing be done in the sanctuary which either offends the eyes of the divine majesty or hinders those who wish to pray there. But in what manner we ought to pray is shown when it is added below.

*When you pray God with psalms and hymns: let that be turned over in the heart which is uttered in the voice.*

The mind of those who sing psalms in church ought to agree with the voice, that the word of the Apostle may be fulfilled: *I will sing with the spirit; I will sing also with the mind [n: (I Cor. XIV)]*. Perseverance in praying only then deserves to be fruitful, if what we pray with the mouth we meditate with the mind. For often we pray and yet direct the heart elsewhere, nor do we recall the very thing which [0892B] we are saying. But God does not hear that prayer to which he who prays does not attend; which is often wont to happen at the devil's prompting. For knowing the usefulness of praying, and envying us the grace of obtaining, he sends upon those who pray tumults of thoughts, that he may divide the mind from prayer and take away the fruit of prayer. Against his malice we ought to have constancy of mind, so that the more the crowd of thoughts assails us, the more sturdily our mind may remain fixed in the uprightness of its own state.
